Naqareh為膜鳴樂器，圓背鼓身以陶土燒製，鼓面覆處理獸皮，以繩索沿鼓緣張緊於: The naqareh is a membranophone: the round-backed body is fired from clay, the head is covered with treated hide, and rope runs round the rim and tightens it against the bowl-shaped back. The Iranian desarkutan uses cowhide, formerly boar hide, tightened with thongs made from ox tendon; the Uzbek koshnaqara is a clay pot with a goatskin head; the Georgian diplipito is a clay pot covered with hide and laced with rope. Some beaters are short wooden sticks; the source states no other parts.
坐或站，將鼓置於身前合適位置。將鼓穩定放置於地面或夾於雙腿之間。用手掌或鼓棒敲擊: Sit or stand and set the drum in a comfortable position in front of you. Rest it firmly on the ground or hold it between the knees. Strike the centre or the edge of the head with the palm or a beater, since different places give different timbres. How hard you strike sets the volume. The sound is made by striking, so watch where you strike and how hard.

納卡雷鼓屬膜鳴樂器，圓背蒙皮，多成對演奏。來源提到它可見於伊拉克馬卡姆查爾吉合奏: The naqareh is a membranophone with a round back and a hide head, usually played in pairs. The source records it in the Iraqi maqam chalghi ensemble, at festivals and weddings in northern Iran, in the Nabat nine-instrument ensemble, in wedding music of northern India, in Ottoman mehter military music, and for song and dance rhythms in Georgian folk ensembles; small ones are also used in modern orchestral ensembles.
納卡雷鼓是中東一帶的膜鳴樂器，屬壺鼓類，通常成對使用。鼓身圓背多以陶土製成，鼓面: The naqareh is a membranophone of the Middle East, a goblet drum, usually played in pairs. The round-backed body is mostly made of fired clay and the head of treated hide, tightened by rope that runs round the rim and over the bowl-shaped back. It is played with two short wooden beaters whose upper ends curve outwards, one drum giving the low note and one the high. It is common in Iraqi maqam ensembles, at Iranian festivals and weddings, in wedding music of northern India, and in European medieval military music, chamber music, dance and processional music.
納卡雷鼓為中東膜鳴鼓，圓背蒙皮，常成對演奏。其名源自烏爾都語動詞「打擊」。13世: The naqareh is a Middle Eastern membranophone with a round back and a hide head, often played in pairs. Its name comes from the Urdu verb for "to strike". In the thirteenth century the Crusaders met Saracen musicians and carried it to Europe; the French nacaire, the Italian naccheroni and the English naker all derive from it. It reached England in the fourteenth century and was used in 1347 in Edward III's procession into Calais; it faded out in the seventeenth century, and the later timpani descend from drums of this kind. In Iraq it is used in the maqam chalghi ensemble, and under the late Abbasid and Fatimid dynasties it was struck before each of the five daily prayers. In India it is called nagara, belongs to the nine-instrument ensemble, today accompanies the Indian oboe shehnai, and once served as a war drum.
納卡雷鼓音色明亮而富有穿透力，具有清晰的打擊感。其圓形的鍋狀共鳴室結構使聲音具有: The naqareh has a bright, penetrating timbre with a clear attack. Its round, pot-shaped resonating chamber gives the sound a warm low-middle foundation while keeping the sharp edge of a struck head. The instrument sits low, and in normal playing its pitch range is limited, but the resonance is deep and lasting. Played in pairs it makes rich layers, the two timbres interweaving into a lively rhythmic texture. Compared with the Western timpani it is drier and more direct, less opulent in resonance; compared with a simple drum it has better tone quality and deeper resonance. Its particular membranophone sound combines the crispness of percussion with the roundness of a pot drum, and it plays an important rhythmic role in Middle Eastern music.
